cited_works.title: Chemiexcitation in Ex Vivo Porcine Skin Model
cited_works.abstract: Chemiexcitation, the formation of electronically excited states via oxidative chemical reactions, has emerged as a potentially important contributor to skin photobiology beyond direct damage caused by ultraviolet (UV) radiation. This study investigates the hypothesis that UV radiation induces chemiexcitation in skin through the formation of triplet excited carbonyls, which may transfer energy to melanin and contribute to oxidative stress even after the termination of UV exposure. Using porcine skin as a model, we demonstrate that UV exposure leads to lipid peroxidation and the subsequent formation of organic radicals, including carbon-centered (alkyl) and oxygen-centered (peroxyl and alkoxyl) species, as detected by EPR spin-trapping spectroscopy. HPLC-MS analysis revealed that short-chain carbonyl compounds, such as formaldehyde and acetaldehyde, are the predominant electronically excited species in direct chemiexcitation. These triplet carbonyls can transfer their excitation energy to melanin through photon emission (radiative transfer) or direct electron exchange (non-radiative transfer), forming melanin-based secondary excited states via indirect chemiexcitation. These findings highlight a novel, light-independent mechanism of post-UV exposure oxidative damage in the skin and suggest a possible role for chemiexcitation in processes such as photoaging and photocarcinogenesis.

cited_works.title: Integrating Ultra-Weak Photon Emission Analysis in Mitochondrial Research
cited_works.abstract: Once regarded solely as the energy source of the cell, nowadays mitochondria are recognized to perform multiple essential functions in addition to energy production. Since the discovery of pathogenic mitochondrial DNA defects in the 1980s, research advances have revealed an increasing number of common human diseases, which share an underlying pathogenesis involving mitochondrial dysfunction. A major factor in this dysfunction is reactive oxygen species (ROS), which influence the mitochondrial-nuclear crosstalk and the link with the epigenome, an influence that provides explanations for pathogenic mechanisms. Regarding these mechanisms, we should take into account that mitochondria produce the majority of ultra-weak photon emission (UPE), an aspect that is often ignored - this type of emission may serve as assay for ROS, thus providing new opportunities for a non-invasive diagnosis of mitochondrial dysfunction. In this article, we overviewed three relevant areas of mitochondria-related research over the period 1960-2020: (a) respiration and energy production, (b) respiration-related production of free radicals and other ROS species, and (c) ultra-weak photon emission in relation to ROS and stress. First, we have outlined how these research areas initially developed independently of each other - following that, our review aims to show their stepwise integration during later stages of development. It is suggested that a further stimulation of research on UPE may have the potential to enhance the progress of modern mitochondrial research and its integration in medicine.

cited_works.title: Mechanism of the Formation of Electronically Excited Species by Oxidative Metabolic Processes: Role of Reactive Oxygen Species
cited_works.abstract: It is well known that biological systems, such as microorganisms, plants, and animals, including human beings, form spontaneous electronically excited species through oxidative metabolic processes. Though the mechanism responsible for the formation of electronically excited species is still not clearly understood, several lines of evidence suggest that reactive oxygen species (ROS) are involved in the formation of electronically excited species. This review attempts to describe the role of ROS in the formation of electronically excited species during oxidative metabolic processes. Briefly, the oxidation of biomolecules, such as lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids by ROS initiates a cascade of reactions that leads to the formation of triplet excited carbonyls formed by the decomposition of cyclic (1,2-dioxetane) and linear (tetroxide) high-energy intermediates. When chromophores are in proximity to triplet excited carbonyls, the triplet-singlet and triplet-triplet energy transfers from triplet excited carbonyls to chromophores result in the formation of singlet and triplet excited chromophores, respectively. Alternatively, when molecular oxygen is present, the triplet-singlet energy transfer from triplet excited carbonyls to molecular oxygen initiates the formation of singlet oxygen. Understanding the mechanism of the formation of electronically excited species allows us to use electronically excited species as a marker for oxidative metabolic processes in cells.

statement: The photon degeneracy parameter delta (mean photon occupation per electromagnetic mode, delta = L_nu * lambda^2) of spontaneous UPE is below 1e-15 in every biological preparation, which places the Hanbury-Brown-Twiss bunching excess of any photocount experiment more than ten orders of magnitude below its own shot noise, so no photocount statistic measured on spontaneous UPE can discriminate a coherent from a chaotic field at any achievable integration time.

scope.population: Three standard preparations measured under one calibration: germinating Vigna radiata (mung bean) beds, log-phase aerobic Saccharomyces cerevisiae cultures, and dark-adapted human dorsal hand skin.
scope.condition: Spontaneous (unstimulated) emission in a temperature-clamped (+/-0.05 C) light-tight chamber, absolute spectral radiance measured in 0.1 nm resolution elements across 350-900 nm with a traceably calibrated optical train of known etendue.
scope.comparator: A traceable low-flux transfer standard (attenuated LED / radioluminescent source, calibrated to <5% at ~1e-16 W) measured through the identical optical train and etendue, plus the matched dark run.
scope.outcome: Absolute spectral photon radiance L_nu (photons s-1 cm-2 sr-1 Hz-1), the derived degeneracy delta = L_nu * lambda^2, and the HBT integration time tau = 36/(delta^2 * Delta_nu) implied for SNR = 3.

null_hypothesis: Some preparation yields delta >= 1e-15 in at least one 0.1 nm resolution element between 350 and 900 nm, or a mode-counted intensity-correlation measurement on that preparation returns g2(0)-1 significantly larger than 1/M for the independently measured mode number M. Either result kills the claim and re-opens the photocount route.
estimand: delta = L_nu * lambda^2, dimensionless photons per mode, with 95% CI, reported per 0.1 nm resolution element and as the band maximum; secondary estimand is the implied SNR=3 integration time tau.
proposed_experiment: Run one traceable radiometric campaign, not a statistics campaign. Calibrate the whole optical train (aperture, solid angle, filter transmission, detector QE, dead time) against a transfer standard traceable to a national metrology institute at the 1e-16 W level. For each of the three preparations, record absolute spectral photon radiance in 0.1 nm resolution elements across 350-900 nm using a grating spectrograph fed to a >90% QE back-illuminated EMCCD photon counter, with interleaved dark and standard-source runs. Report delta = L_nu*lambda^2 per resolution element with uncertainty budget. Then, as a confirmatory arm, run a two-channel HBT on the brightest preparation with the mode number M independently fixed by a single-mode fibre plus a 0.1 nm filter, measure g2(0)-1 and check it against the 1/M prediction and against the delta-derived SNR bound. Pre-register the 1e-15 threshold and the equivalence test.

rationale.step: The field's own critical review states that claims about UPE statistical properties are very controversial and closes by hoping that detectors closer to ideal may bring at least partial answers; a separate UPE review states outright that photocount statistics cannot discriminate a coherent from a thermal state when many modes are collected.

Measured spontaneous UPE flux is a few to some hundred photons per second per square centimetre of surface (10-1e3 photons cm-2 s-1 over 200-1000 nm in recent EMCCD imaging), and a whole cell-culture dish gives roughly 12 photons per second; the emission goes into approximately 2*pi sr over a 350-900 nm continuum.

Compute delta for the optimistic case. Take 1e3 photons s-1 cm-2 into 2*pi sr, lambda = 600 nm, Delta_lambda = 400 nm. Optical bandwidth Delta_nu = c*Delta_lambda/lambda^2 = (3e10 cm/s)(4e-5 cm)/(3.6e-9 cm^2) = 3.3e14 Hz. Photon radiance L = 1e3/(2*pi) = 1.6e2 photons s-1 cm-2 sr-1. Spectral photon radiance L_nu = 1.6e2/3.3e14 = 4.8e-13 photons s-1 cm-2 sr-1 Hz-1. Single-mode etendue = lambda^2 = 3.6e-9 cm^2 sr. Therefore delta = L_nu * lambda^2 = 1.7e-21 photons per mode.

Compute the resulting HBT sensitivity. For chaotic light with M detected modes the fractional bunching excess is g2(0)-1 = 1/M and the excess-to-noise after time tau, at bin T, is SNR = sqrt(R1*R2*T*tau)*(g2(0)-1). Substituting R = delta*Delta_nu*M_spatial and T = 1/Delta_nu (ideal single-temporal-mode timing) gives the mode-independent result SNR = (delta/2)*sqrt(Delta_nu*tau). Setting SNR = 3 with delta = 1.7e-21 and Delta_nu = 3.3e14 Hz gives tau = 36/(delta^2*Delta_nu) = 4e28 s, roughly 1e11 times the age of the universe. Because M_spatial cancels, narrowband filtering, single-mode-fibre selection and light concentration are exactly SNR-neutral: no optical arrangement rescues the measurement.

The corpus contains both signs of this geometry dependence stated qualitatively rather than computed: hand UPE was reported to lack the usual coherence because of the large area and the long measurement time, while 20000-bin photocount fits yielding squeezed parameters were performed in exactly the same many-mode regime with a broadband 300-800 nm detector.

Theory in the corpus establishes that stationary light built from randomly timed emissions acquires the correlation properties of chaotic light in the strong-overlap limit regardless of the statistics of the individual emitters, so the chaotic-light SNR formula above is the correct upper bound for any UPE source model, coherent sub-emitters included.

A field in a genuinely coherent state in the sense claimed by the coherence literature is a macroscopically occupied mode, i.e. delta >= 1. Measuring delta by absolute radiometry therefore tests the coherence claim with a first-order (intensity, etendue, bandwidth) measurement whose sensitivity scales as sqrt(N) rather than as delta, making it ~1e20 times more sensitive than any g2 route; existing calibrated photon-counting radiometry, where detector noise already dominates source photon noise, is adequate to do it.

Light-concentration schemes that raise collected flux (high-albedo integrating cavity with 50% number efficiency) do so by scrambling angle and therefore raise M in exact proportion, confirming operationally that flux gain cannot buy bunching contrast.

cited_works.title: Low‐level luminescence of the human skin
cited_works.abstract: BACKGROUND/AIMS/METHODS: For the first time systematic measurements of the low-level luminescence of the human skin ("bi-ophotons") have been performed by means of a photon detector device set up in darkness. RESULTS: Several months of daily investigations have shown that body light emission follows definite and well-known biological rhythms, such as 14 days, 1 month, 3 months, 9 months, and reflects the left-right symmetry of the body. The results confirm that biophotons are related to physiological functions. CONCLUSIONS: This technique provides a new and powerful noninvasive diagnostic method. In particular, skin research and development may use it for testing the influence of different skin treatments.

cited_works.abstract: We explored the patterns of biophoton-ultra-weak light made by cells-emissions in Neuro-2a cells and astrocytes in culture. Biophotons were detected using a photomultiplier as a single photon counter. We measured intensity of emissions when healthy (and at rest), stressed with toxins (sodium troclosene or rotenone) and/or treated with red and near infrared light (R-NIr). We measured ATP (adenosine triphosphate) and ROS (reactive oxygen species) levels also. Our results showed that emissions from Neuro-2a cells and astrocytes were similar when both healthy and stressed. Both cell types emitted biophotons at low intensities when healthy (~ 12 photons/s), but this changed markedly under stress. The extent of change was however, dependant on the stressor involved; at the concentrations we used, sodium troclosene increased emissions, while rotenone had a far more limited impact. Finally, we showed that R-NIr did not influence emissions when healthy, but did so when stressed, particularly with sodium troclosene. Under our experimental time-lines, these emission patterns under different conditions did not relate uniformly to the changes in ATP and ROS levels. In summary, we found that biophoton emissions did not readily define cell type, but could-under some circumstances-be reflective of cell health. Further, that R-NIr could influence these emissions, particularly under stress.

cited_works.title: Imaging Ultraweak Photon Emission from Living and Dead Mice and from Plants under Stress
cited_works.abstract: The phenomenon of biological ultraweak photon emission (UPE), that is, extremely low-intensity emission (10 − 10 3 photons/cm 2 /sec) in the spectral range of 200 − 1000 nm, has been observed in all living systems that have been examined. Here we report experiments that exemplify the ability of novel imaging systems to detect variations in UPE for a set of physiologically important scenarios. We use EMCCD and CCD cameras to capture single visible-wavelength photons with low noise and quantum efficiencies higher than 90%. Our investigation reveals significant contrast between the UPE from live vs. dead mice. In plants we observed that an increase in temperature and injuries both caused an increase in UPE intensity. Moreover, chemical treatments modified the UPE emission characteristics of plants, particularly the application of an anesthetic (benzocaine) to injury, which showed the highest emission among the compounds tested. As a result, UPE imaging provides the possibility of non-invasive label-free imaging of vitality in animals and the responses of plants to stress.

cited_works.title: Coherence and photon statistics for optical fields generated by Poisson random emissions
cited_works.abstract: We examine the coherence properties and photon statistics of stationary light obtained by the superposition of nonstationary emissions occurring at random times, in accordance with a homogeneous Poisson point process. The individual emissions are assumed to be in a coherent, chaotic, or $n$ state. The statistical nature of the emission times results in fluctuations of the relative contributions of different emissions at a given time. This is manifested by an additional positive term, exhibiting particlelike properties, in the normalized second-order correlation function. Thus, the photon-counting variance is increased. For coherent emissions, interference between the randomly delayed emissions produces additional wavelike noise. In the limit when the emissions overlap strongly, the field exhibits the correlation properties of chaotic light, regardless of the statistics of the individual emissions. In the opposite limit, when emissions seldom overlap, the light intensity is describable by a shot-noise stochastic process, and the detected photocounts show an enhanced particlelike noise, which has its largest value when the counting time is long. In that limit, the photocounts obey the Neyman type-$A$ and generalized Polya-Aeppli distributions, when the individual emissions are coherent and chaotic, respectively. When the individual emissions correspond to the $n$ state, the Poisson emission times result in bunching which reduces or eliminates the inherent antibunching associated with the $n$ state.

rationale.step: The coherence claim under debate is explicitly a claim about the state of the field: that delayed luminescence and steady-state UPE exhibit mode coupling over the entire spectrum and originate from fully coherent and sometimes squeezed states. A claim about phase coherence is a first-order claim, but the field has only ever tested it with second-order (intensity) statistics.

Compute the sensitivity asymmetry between the two routes. Fringe visibility is estimated from the detected intensity, so its shot-noise error is sigma_V ~ N^-1/2 on N total detected photons, whereas the intensity-correlation route's SNR scales as delta (see Q2-1). At 1e2-1e3 counts s-1 and 1e5 s, N = 1e7-1e8 and sigma_V = 1e-4 to 3e-4 before etendue restriction. Applying the Jacquinot limit Omega <= 2*pi/R with R = lambda/dlambda = 6000 costs roughly 1e-4 of the flux, leaving sigma_V ~ 1e-2 after one day and ~3e-3 after ten days. The required-time ratio between the first-order and second-order routes is therefore of order 1e20-1e23.

Compute what linewidth the coherence claim demands. Coherence length l_c = lambda^2/Delta_lambda. At lambda = 600 nm: Delta_lambda = 400 nm gives l_c = 0.9 um and tau_c = 3 fs; Delta_lambda = 1 nm gives l_c = 0.36 mm and tau_c = 1.2 ps. Coherence across a single cell (10 um) already requires Delta_lambda <= 36 nm; coherence across an organism (10 cm) requires Delta_lambda <= 3.6e-6 nm. The claim is therefore a spectroscopic linewidth claim with a concrete resolution target.

No work in the corpus has resolved a UPE spectrum better than about 10 nm: plant chemiluminescence is characterised by bandpass or cut-off filters (450-850 nm in vitro, red/far-red > 640 nm peaking 700-750 nm in planta; 50 nm bandpass increments in Arabidopsis; 550 nm and 495 nm cut-off ratios in human fingertips; > 650 nm in wounded Spathiphyllum). The narrow-line hypothesis has therefore never been given a chance to fail.

Instrument-side confounds that would fake a narrow feature are documented and controllable: photomultiplier dynode and support-structure light emission with a characterisable spectrum, and the general artifact risk from lacking or improper reference signals in UPE statistics work. The positive/negative control arms are designed against exactly these.

cited_works.title: Properties of biophotons and their theoretical implications.
cited_works.abstract: The word "biophotons" is used to denote a permanent spontaneous photon emission from all living systems. It displays a few up to some hundred photons/(s x cm2) within the spectral range from at least 260 to 800 nm. It is closely linked to delayed luminescence (DL) of biological tissues which describes the long term and ultra weak reemission of photons after exposure to light illumination. During relaxation DL turns continuously into the steady state biophoton emission, where both, DL and biophoton emission exhibit mode coupling over the entire spectrum and a Poissonian photo count distribution. DL is representing excited states of the biophoton field. The physical properties indicate that biophotons originate from fully coherent and sometimes even squeezed states. The physical analysis provides thermodynamic and quantum optical interpretation, in order to understand the biological impacts of biophotons. Biological phenomena like intracellular and intercellular communication, cell growth and differentiation, interactions among biological systems (like "Gestaltbildung" or swarming), and microbial infections can be understood in terms of biophotons. "Biophotonics", the corresponding field of applications, provide a new powerful tool for assessing the quality of food (like freshness and shelf life), microbial infections, environmental influences and for substantiating medical diagnosis and therapy.

cited_works.title: Light Induced Afterpulses in Photomultipliers
cited_works.abstract: Various spurious effects limit the effectiveness of Photomultipliers when used in low-light-level coincidence counting experiments. cited_works.title: Short-time fractal analysis of biological autoluminescence
cited_works.abstract: Biological systems manifest continuous weak autoluminescence, which is present even in the absence of external stimuli. Since this autoluminescence arises from internal metabolic and physiological processes, several works suggested that it could carry information in the time series of the detected photon counts. Utilizing the fractional Brownian bridge that employs short samples of time series in the method kernel, we suggest that the detected autoluminescence signal from mung beans is not totally random, but it seems to involve a process with a negative memory. Our results contribute to the development of the rigorous methodology of signal analysis of photonic biosignals.

rationale.step: Superposition of nonstationary emissions occurring at Poisson-random times produces exactly Neyman type-A photocount distributions (coherent sub-emissions) or generalised Polya-Aeppli distributions (chaotic sub-emissions), with enhanced particle-like noise and increased photon-counting variance. This is a purely classical mechanism that manufactures the 'quantum-looking' excess.

Clustering is directly observed in an ultraweak biological emission: photomultiplier pulses from human breath chemiluminescence arrive in bursts, which the authors attribute to chain reactions, long-lived emitters, or both.

In PMA-stimulated neutrophils the Fano factor of the true UPE signal rises with counting-window size while randomly shuffled surrogates of the same signal do not - the defining signature of a clustered point process rather than of a state of the field.

The chain chemistry is manipulable in exactly these preparations: UPE arises from ROS-driven lipid and protein oxidation via triplet excited carbonyls and singlet oxygen; it falls under anoxia and under topical antioxidants (glutathione, tocopherol, ascorbate, CoQ10), and linoleic-acid-induced emission in Chlamydomonas is suppressed by hydroxyl-radical scavenging (mannitol), by lipoxygenase inhibition (catechol) and by removal of molecular oxygen; wound-induced leaf emission is suppressed under anoxia. Yeast BAL is likewise driven by Fenton-generated ROS and tracks oxygen partial pressure.

The squeezed-state reading rests on a three-parameter fit (signal strength plus r = 0.06, theta = 2.76, phi = 0.64) claimed to reproduce photocount distributions across 50 ms to 6 s bins from 20000 measurements. The cluster model makes the same multi-bin prediction with two parameters and, unlike r/theta/phi, its parameters carry a chemical interpretation that can be perturbed - which is what makes the comparison decisive rather than aesthetic.

Derive the discriminating signature. For a Neyman type-A process the Fano factor at bin T much longer than the cluster duration is F = 1 + mu, independent of lambda_c, while for T much shorter than the cluster duration F tends to 1. The prediction is a sigmoidal F(T) whose plateau height equals mu and whose knee locates the chain duration - a shape no squeezed-state parameterisation predicts. A published seed measurement gives <n> = 27.25 with variance 34.01, i.e. F = 1.25, corresponding to mu = 0.25 detected photons per cluster, i.e. mu/eta = 2.5 emitted photons per initiation at eta = 0.1: a chemically plausible chain yield and a directly falsifiable number.

cited_works.title: Coherence and photon statistics for optical fields generated by Poisson random emissions
cited_works.abstract: We examine the coherence properties and photon statistics of stationary light obtained by the superposition of nonstationary emissions occurring at random times, in accordance with a homogeneous Poisson point process. The individual emissions are assumed to be in a coherent, chaotic, or $n$ state. The statistical nature of the emission times results in fluctuations of the relative contributions of different emissions at a given time. This is manifested by an additional positive term, exhibiting particlelike properties, in the normalized second-order correlation function. Thus, the photon-counting variance is increased. For coherent emissions, interference between the randomly delayed emissions produces additional wavelike noise. In the limit when the emissions overlap strongly, the field exhibits the correlation properties of chaotic light, regardless of the statistics of the individual emissions. In the opposite limit, when emissions seldom overlap, the light intensity is describable by a shot-noise stochastic process, and the detected photocounts show an enhanced particlelike noise, which has its largest value when the counting time is long. In that limit, the photocounts obey the Neyman type-$A$ and generalized Polya-Aeppli distributions, when the individual emissions are coherent and chaotic, respectively. When the individual emissions correspond to the $n$ state, the Poisson emission times result in bunching which reduces or eliminates the inherent antibunching associated with the $n$ state.

cited_works.abstract: Human breath spontaneously emits photons at a rate of approximately 7,000/liter-s. The emission has a peak in the red part of the spectrum and an ultraviolet contribution. cited_works.title: Biological autoluminescence for assessing oxidative processes in yeast cell cultures
cited_works.abstract: Nowadays, modern medicine is looking for new, more gentle, and more efficient diagnostic methods. Coherence becomes classical if the agent causing cooperation is discernible otherwise it is quantum coherence. cited_works.title: Revisiting Claims of Extracranial Biophoton Detection from the Human Brain
cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.

cited_works.title: Short-time fractal analysis of biological autoluminescence
cited_works.abstract: Biological systems manifest continuous weak autoluminescence, which is present even in the absence of external stimuli. Since this autoluminescence arises from internal metabolic and physiological processes, several works suggested that it could carry information in the time series of the detected photon counts. However, there is little experimental work which would show any difference of this signal from random Poisson noise and some works were prone to artifacts due to lacking or improper reference signals. Here we apply rigorous statistical methods and advanced reference signals to test the hypothesis whether time series of autoluminescence from germinating mung beans display any intrinsic correlations. Utilizing the fractional Brownian bridge that employs short samples of time series in the method kernel, we suggest that the detected autoluminescence signal from mung beans is not totally random, but it seems to involve a process with a negative memory. Our results contribute to the development of the rigorous methodology of signal analysis of photonic biosignals.

statement: No photocount or temporal-complexity feature of UPE - Fano factor, Mandel Q, kurtosis, Hurst/fractional-Brownian exponent, diffusion-entropy scaling exponent, or entropy-weighted spectral fractal dimension - adds more than 0.02 AUC out-of-sample to a classifier of biological state that already contains log mean count rate plus chamber temperature and background rate.

scope.population: Two pre-registered discrimination tasks, each with an independent held-out cohort acquired after the model is frozen: (a) glioblastoma versus astrocyte cell cultures; (b) viable versus degenerated or frozen mouse embryos, and as a second clinical arm healthy versus type-2-diabetic human hand skin.
scope.condition: Blinded analysis of fixed-length photon-count time series (identical acquisition length, bin grid and spectral band across classes), with chamber temperature and interleaved dark-reference rate logged as covariates.
scope.comparator: An intensity-only baseline model containing log mean count rate plus the same covariates, fitted and evaluated on identical folds.
scope.outcome: delta-AUC on the held-out cohort between the full-feature model and the intensity-only baseline.

null_hypothesis: delta-AUC > 0.02 with a lower 95% confidence bound above 0 on a genuinely held-out cohort. That would show photocount statistics carry state information beyond intensity and would falsify the claim.
estimand: delta-AUC (held-out) between full-feature and intensity-only models, with 95% CI from nested cross-fitting plus an external cohort; reported per task and pooled.
proposed_experiment: Pre-register the feature list, the baseline covariates, the equivalence threshold (delta-AUC = 0.02) and the analysis code before any held-out data are acquired. Acquire matched-length photon-count time series for both classes in each task under identical bin grid, spectral band and acquisition length, with in-chamber temperature and an interleaved dark-reference channel recorded continuously. Fit the intensity-only baseline and the full-feature model on the development cohort with nested cross-fitting, freeze both, then evaluate once on the externally acquired held-out cohort. Report delta-AUC with CI, plus a rate-matched subsample analysis in which classes are trimmed to overlapping log-mean-rate distributions. No new detector is needed; the claim is a design-and-analysis claim and is testable on re-analysis of any existing dataset that retained raw time series and rate logs.

rationale.step: Multiple groups report that temporal-statistical features separate biological states: diffusion entropy analysis separating astrocyte from glioblastoma cultures; anomalous DEA scaling appearing with germinating seeds present but ordinary scaling in dark counts; a fractional-Brownian negative-memory signature in mung-bean autoluminescence; an entropy-weighted spectral fractal dimension distinguishing living from degenerated and frozen from fresh mouse embryos; non-zero kurtosis in healthy and diabetic photocount distributions; and spectral power density profiles yielding 90% discriminant accuracy for malignancy.

In none of those studies is the comparison made against an intensity-matched baseline, yet mean intensity is itself an established correlate of the same states: tumour cells emit more than non-malignant cells, stressed cells emit more than healthy ones, and UPE intensity tracks ROS production and oxidative status generally.

The one UPE study in the corpus that used surrogate randomisation for a physiological correlation found the correlations to be temporary, drifting in phase and frequency - the behaviour expected of a shared slow covariate rather than of a stable state-specific feature.

Show the confound is structural, not incidental. Every listed feature is a functional of the same intensity time series and is monotonically biased by mean rate. For a Cox process, Q = <n>*sigma_I^2, so any class difference in mean rate propagates directly into Q and F. Likewise, an estimated Hurst or DEA scaling exponent is pulled toward the uncorrelated value 0.5 as the Poisson shot component grows relative to the rate-fluctuation component, i.e. as <n> falls; the dark-count arm returning ordinary scaling while the seed arm returns anomalous scaling is exactly what this bias predicts when the two arms differ in mean rate. Matching or adjusting on log mean rate is therefore the minimal control, and it has been applied in none of the cited works.

The critical review already frames the whole controversy as one about statistical properties rather than intensity and spectrum, on which there is consensus; so the practical question 'can photocount statistics ever decide anything' is precisely whether these features survive an intensity-matched baseline.

cited_works.abstract: We study the emission of photons from germinating seeds using an experimental technique designed to detect light of extremely small intensity. We analyze the dark count signal without germinating seeds as well as the photon emission during the germination process. The technique of analysis adopted here, called diffusion entropy analysis (DEA) and originally designed to measure the temporal complexity of astrophysical, sociological and physiological processes, rests on Kolmogorov complexity. The updated version of DEA used in this paper is designed to determine if the signal complexity is generated either by non-ergodic crucial events with a non-stationary correlation function or by the infinite memory of a stationary but non-integrable correlation function or by a mixture of both processes. We find that dark count yields the ordinary scaling, thereby showing that no complexity of either kinds may occur without any seeds in the chamber. In the presence of seeds in the chamber anomalous scaling emerges, reminiscent of that found in neuro-physiological processes. However, this is a mixture of both processes and with the progress of germination the non-ergodic component tends to vanish and complexity becomes dominated by the stationary infinite memory. We illustrate some conjectures ranging from stress induced annihilation of crucial events to the emergence of quantum coherence.

cited_works.title: Ultraweak Photon Emissions as a Non-Invasive, Early-Malignancy Detection Tool: An In Vitro and In Vivo Study
cited_works.abstract: Early detection of cancer improves treatment options and increases survival. Building upon previous demonstrations that ultraweak photon emissions (UPE) could be measured to detect cancers, we designed an early detection protocol to test malignancy in both in vitro and in vivo systems. Photons were measured for 100 s from plates containing ~1 million malignant or non-malignant cells from 13 different types of human and mouse cell lines. Tumor cells displayed increased photon emissions compared to non-malignant cells. Examining the standardized Spectral Power Density (SPD) configurations for flux densities between 0.1 and 25 Hz (Δf = 0.01 Hz) yielded 90% discriminant accuracy. The emission profiles of mice that had been injected with melanoma cells could be differentiated from a non-malignant reference groups as early as 24 h post-injection. The peak SPD associated with photon emissions was ~20 Hz for both malignant cell cultures and mice with growing tumors. These results extend the original suggestion by Takeda and his colleagues (2004) published in this journal concerning the potential diagnostic value of UPEs for assessing proliferations of carcinoma cells. We measured ATP (adenosine triphosphate) and ROS (reactive oxygen species) levels also. Our results showed that emissions from Neuro-2a cells and astrocytes were similar when both healthy and stressed. Both cell types emitted biophotons at low intensities when healthy (~ 12 photons/s), but this changed markedly under stress. The extent of change was however, dependant on the stressor involved; at the concentrations we used, sodium troclosene increased emissions, while rotenone had a far more limited impact. Finally, we showed that R-NIr did not influence emissions when healthy, but did so when stressed, particularly with sodium troclosene. Under our experimental time-lines, these emission patterns under different conditions did not relate uniformly to the changes in ATP and ROS levels. In summary, we found that biophoton emissions did not readily define cell type, but could-under some circumstances-be reflective of cell health. Further, that R-NIr could influence these emissions, particularly under stress.

cited_works.abstract: Ultraweak photon emission, also referred to as biological autoluminescence or biophoton emission, is the spontaneous emission of extremely low levels of light from a broad range of biological systems. Recent studies have reported that UPE measured extracranially can serve as a potential noninvasive biomarker of brain activity. Here, we show that this interpretation suffers from serious problems. We show that, when observed under properly dark conditions, the UPE from the head is much weaker than what is reported in certain papers on "brain UPE" from human heads. We also show that the large signals reported in these studies can be explained by background light contamination. Furthermore, photons with wavelengths <600 nm are strongly attenuated by scalp and skull tissues, and longer wavelengths fall largely outside the effective spectral sensitivity of the photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) used. As a consequence, even if UPE from the head is detected under properly background-free conditions, it is likely to be dominated by emission from the scalp rather than from the brain, certainly as long as PMTs are used. Our results emphasize the importance of careful experimental design to make genuine progress on this important question.
